title: What forces the bounds
summary: Every lower bound in the atlas names the resource the adversary exploits. Read side by side, a few bottlenecks (distance, symmetry, missing information, an adversary that acts) explain most tight results, and the open entries cluster where no bottleneck beyond distance is known.

sections.heading: Naming the bottleneck
sections.body:
Each lower bound in the atlas carries a `bottleneck`: two or three words for what the adversary uses. Across all problems the commonest names are *distance*, *symmetry breaking* and *symmetry*, then *memory* (colours of lights), *unknown exit*, *adversarial edge changes* and *unknown distance*; a long tail of names (*trap graphs*, *port addressing*, *indistinguishable Byzantine agents*, *timing is the only channel*) covers single arguments. This essay groups them into four kinds and ends with what is left open.

The grouping matters because results move along the assumption axes in opposite directions: an algorithm for a weak setting holds in every stronger one, a lower bound for a strong setting holds in every weaker one. A bound whose bottleneck survives every strengthening (distance, for instance) is inherited by a whole subtree of settings; a bound that depends on an assumption (asynchrony, an unknown exit) disappears as soon as that assumption is lifted.

sections.heading: Distance: something must travel
sections.body:
The plainest argument is that an entity must cover a distance. Kshemkalyani et al. state it for dispersion in one sentence: "Suppose two nodes of a graph are at a distance of $\Omega(k)$, then to disperse from one node to the furthest node takes $\Omega(k)$ time (e.g., line graph)" [Kshemkalyani2025Almost]. The bound is from [Kshemkalyani2019Efficient], and after several rounds of algorithms it is matched by $O(k)$ rounds, synchronous and asynchronous [Kshemkalyani2025Almost] [Pattanayak2025OptimalAsync]. On grids the distance is $\sqrt k$ [Kshemkalyani2020Grids]. For collaborative exploration the offline cost $\Theta(n/k+D)$ is the distance part [Disser2020General].

Programmable matter has the same argument, counted in moves: $n$ particles reshaping a compact configuration into a line need $\Omega(n^2)$ moves in total [Derakhshandeh2015Leader], as do deterministic shape formation [DiLuna2020Shape], universal coating [Derakhshandeh2017Coating] and centralised transformations by sliding [Michail2019Transformation]; universal shape formation needs $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ rounds [Derakhshandeh2016Universal]. Distance bounds are usually the easy half of a tight result. What took years in dispersion was the algorithm, not the bound.

sections.heading: Symmetry and identity
sections.body:
The second kind of argument is about possibility rather than cost. Identical entities that the adversary keeps in symmetric positions cannot be separated by a deterministic rule: two oblivious robots in SSYNC [Suzuki1999Formation] [Flocchini2016Constant], anonymous agents whose views coincide [Dieudonne2016Anonymous], leader election among disoriented robots in symmetric positions [Dieudonne2013Geoleader], arbitrary patterns in ASYNC without a common orientation [Flocchini2008Arbitrary], and silent particles that share only chirality [Navarra2023Line]. Identical points that the robots cannot count produce the same effect: without multiplicity detection gathering is impossible [Prencipe2007Impossibility].

Even when identifiers break symmetry, carrying them costs memory. For dispersion of $k$ agents the $\Omega(\log k)$ bits bound holds "since at least one agent needs $\Omega(\log k)$ bits to store its unique ID" [Kshemkalyani2025Almost] [Augustine2018Tradeoffs]. Anonymous rendezvous in graphs of $n$ nodes needs $\Theta(\log n)$ bits [Czyzowicz2012Forget], and labelled rendezvous on a ring with simultaneous start takes $\Theta(d\log\lambda)$ rounds, where $d$ is the initial distance between the agents and $\lambda$ the smaller label: the price of reading a label of $\log\lambda$ bits bit by bit [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. When agents cannot talk at all, time is the only channel: silent dispersion needs $\Omega(k+\log L)$ rounds [Das2025SilentRing] and $\Omega(\log L+\log\Delta)$ bits [Gorain2022Silent], with identifiers at most $L$ and maximum degree $\Delta$. In the plane the same economy appears as colours: two robots with lights need two [Viglietta2013Rendezvous], with only internal or only external lights three [Otaka2026TwoState].

sections.heading: Information: not knowing where to go
sections.body:
Search problems are bounded by what the searcher does not know. Beck already showed that, without knowing the distribution of the target, the distance travelled cannot be below 9 times the expected distance (as reported by [Kupavskii2018Lower]), and the cow-path ratio 9 is the competitive form of the same fact [BaezaYates1993Searching]; randomization lowers it to about $4.5911$ [Kao1996Randomized]. Kupavskii and Welzl's bound for $m$ rays, specialised to robots without faults, settled the question of parallel search on $m$ rays "posed by three groups of scientists some 15 to 30 years ago" [Kupavskii2018Lower]. An unknown exit gives every evacuation bound on the disk [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating], and one-way communication gives the line its exact ratio $3+2\sqrt2$ [Czyzowicz2021GroupEvacuation].

On graphs the missing information is which port to take. Remembering one port among $\Delta$ costs $\lceil\log\Delta\rceil$ bits for perpetual tree exploration [Diks2004Tree] and $\Omega(\log\Delta)$ bits for dispersion by anonymous randomized agents [Molla2019Randomness]; treasure hunt with pebbles needs $\Omega(D\log\Delta)$ rounds [Gorain2022Pebble]. Stronger memory bounds come from trap graphs, built so that an agent with too little memory (or too few pebbles) misses part of them: $\Omega(D\log\Delta)$ bits for perpetual exploration [Fraigniaud2005Automaton] and $\Theta(\log\log n)$ pebbles for a constant-memory agent [Disser2019Pebbles]. Fraigniaud et al. recall why these bounds were pursued: exploration by finite automata was tied to the complexity of undirected connectivity [Fraigniaud2006Reduced].

sections.heading: Adversaries that act
sections.body:
Some bounds need an adversary that does more than choose the input. An adversary that removes edges forces three agents and $\Omega(n^{1.5})$ moves for black hole search in a dynamic ring [DiLuna2025DynamicBHS], makes dispersion with local communication impossible in 1-interval-connected graphs [Kshemkalyani2020Dynamic], and forces $\Omega(n^2)$ steps to explore some temporal graphs even offline, whereas static undirected graphs need fewer than $2n$ [Erlebach2021Temporal]. An adversary that delays agents forces $\Theta(n^2)$ moves in black hole search without a map [Dobrev2006Searching] and an $\Omega(\log^2 k)$ factor in asynchronous collaborative tree exploration [Cosson2025Asynchronous]; one that reveals a tree online forces a competitive ratio of $\Omega(\log k/\log\log k)$ for collaborative exploration [Disser2020General].

Byzantine entities act from inside. Because they are indistinguishable from good ones, gathering on graphs with $f$ Byzantine agents needs $f+1$ good agents [Bouchard2016Byzantine], three robots with one Byzantine cannot gather in SSYNC [Agmon2006Fault], dispersion of $k > n$ agents on $n$ nodes into a balanced configuration is impossible whenever $\lceil k/n\rceil > \lceil (k-f)/n\rceil$, because Byzantine agents can occupy nodes exactly like honest ones [Molla2021ByzantineGraphs], and the best lower bound for search on the line with Byzantine robots, about $5.23$, comes from the argument for crash faults [Kupavskii2018Lower]. The black hole is the extreme case of an adversary inside the network: an asynchronous team without a map needs $\Delta+1$ agents, $\Delta$ the maximum degree, and it cannot succeed at all if $n$ is unknown or the graph is not 2-connected [Dobrev2006Searching].

sections.heading: Where the gaps are
sections.body:
At the time of writing, the atlas judges optimality per measure for every variant, and more than two in five of these judgements are *unknown*: no non-trivial lower bound, or no analysis of that measure. Most of them come from two habits of the literature. In the plane, time is often not analysed because the question was feasibility. On graphs, rendezvous and exploration algorithms often leave memory unbounded. Both are open questions that nobody has asked yet rather than hard ones.

The polynomial gaps cluster where the only lower bound is distance. Dispersion on trees with $n$ nodes has $O(n)$ for $k=n$ agents against an $\Omega(D^2)$ bound proved only for trees of height about $\sqrt{\log n}$ [Disser2020General]; crash-tolerant dispersion is a factor $\Delta$ (the maximum degree) from $\Omega(k)$ [Pattanayak2023Spite]; Byzantine dispersion is $\tilde O(n^9)$ against $\Omega(n)$ [Molla2021ByzantineGraphs]. Black hole search with tokens is $O(mn)$, for $m$ edges, against $\Omega(n^2/\Delta)$ [Balamohan2016Tokens]. Stopping tree exploration without knowing $n$ uses $O(\log n)$ bits against an $\Omega(\log\log\log n)$ bound [Ambuhl2011Tree] [Diks2004Tree], and leader election in programmable matter has no proven lower bound, only an informal $\Omega(D)$ remark, $D$ being the diameter of the particle configuration [Dufoulon2021Efficient]. Where the bottleneck is symmetry or missing information, results tend to be tight or exact; the gaps that remain in search are between two constants, as in two-robot face-to-face evacuation, about $5.255$ against $5.6234$ [Czyzowicz2020FaceToFace] [Disser2019Second]. The progress map of each problem shows the bottleneck next to every bound, so these patterns can be checked directly.
